title: With so many unsold homes, should first-time buyers still buy?
videoTitle: OVERSUPPLY? EXPENSIVE RENT!! HOW TO NAVIGATE THE MARKET AS A FIRST TIME HOME BUYER??
excerpt: Headlines about 33,000 unsold homes scare first-time buyers while their rent keeps rising. Sean looks at where the unsold units are, and what to weigh before buying an affordable home.

qa.context: News and influencers keep citing about 33,000 unsold homes in Malaysia, about 52,000 with serviced apartments. First-time buyers hear that the market is oversupplied and wait, while the rent they pay their landlord goes up every year.
qa.question: Does the oversupply mean first-time buyers should hold off, and are capped-price affordable homes a safe first purchase?
qa.quote: Right location, wrong price, you still lose money.
qa.answer: Oversupply is real but local, and it doesn't mean property in demand areas is cheap. Judge a purchase by entry price first, location second and timing third, and don't buy an affordable home just because the price is capped.

reasons.title: The unsold homes are concentrated
reasons.body: About 65% of the unsold units are priced under RM500,000 and about 12,000 under RM300,000, led by Johor, Selangor and Perak. Sean suspects many are government affordable projects in smaller towns, while in JB or KL a home under RM500,000 sells easily.

reasons.title: Rents show the real demand
reasons.body: Rents have risen roughly 12% to 18% around KLCC, 18% to 25% in Mont Kiara, 15% to 22% in Taman Melawati, 14% to 20% in Subang Jaya and 10% to 16% in Shah Alam over about five years. Even in Medini, long called oversupplied, rents rose about 50% once new supply stopped.

reasons.title: Entry price beats location
reasons.body: Buy in the right place at the wrong price and you lose money, or at best wait 10 to 15 years to recover. Buy below the area's median, even in a lesser town, and it can still pay. Time your own circumstances rather than the market.

reasons.title: Affordable homes have catches
reasons.body: A capped price of RM300,000 can still be expensive in an outskirt town. Some schemes add RM35,000 to RM55,000 in compulsory fittings, about 20% upfront, and a moratorium stops you selling or renting, so exiting a residential-only location can be hard.

actions: Check oversupply for the exact town you are buying in, using NAPIC's downloadable data, not the national headline.
Compare rents in the area over the past five years before deciding whether it is really oversupplied.
Pay at or below the area's median transacted price, whatever the location.
If you qualify for an affordable home, compare locations and layouts rather than taking the first one offered.
Given the choice, pick an affordable unit blended into an open-market project, which shares its facilities and should rent better once the moratorium ends.
qa.caveat: Budget 2027 helps buyers under RM500,000 with lower stamp duty, SJKP guarantees for irregular incomes and a second LPPSA loan for civil servants, so some of the unsold stock may clear. Sean's view of affordable homes as an investment is cautious, not a ban: if you are entitled to one in a good location, it can make sense.
